Theme

Civic life: news, government & the law

population noun

the people living in a place, and their number

also inhabitants, number of inhabitants, census, population count, head count, densely populated, densely populated region

classical

Liv. 1.44.3: ad eam multitūdinem urbs quoque amplificanda vīsa est
Traupman 205, 363: population; numerus omnis multitūdinis, the total population
Traupman 203

multitūdō, multitūdinis f.

noun, third declension

the population: the number of people

Livy’s word for the people a city holds, or hopes to hold; with numerus for the figure.

Other words

  • incolae, incolārum m. pl. — the inhabitants, the residents

    noun, first declension, plural · also used · classical · Liv. 22.46.9: regiōnis incolae; M-O s.v. population: incolārum numerus

    Lewis & Short: an inhabitant, a resident, as against a citizen. Morgan–Owens counts a population as the number of its inhabitants.

  • 1lūstrum: long u (Lewis & Short leaves it unmarked). De Vaan, s.v. lūstrum, “ceremony of purification; five-year period”, from *luH- “set free” (luō); distinct from lustrum, a muddy place, a den.

    cēnsus1, cēnsūs m. — the Roman census: the count of the citizens and their property

    noun, fourth declension · also used · classical · Liv. 1.44.2: mīlia octōgintā eō lūstrō cīvium cēnsa dīcuntur; Caes. BG 1.29.3: cēnsū habitō

    Taken by the censors every five years and closed by the purification, the lūstrum (Lewis & Short); the result is given as cēnsa cīvium capita, the citizens counted (Liv. 3.24.10). Caesar uses the word for a count of the Helvetii.

  • recēnsus, recēnsūs m. — a count of the people; a census

    noun, fourth declension · also used · classical · Suet. Caes. 41.3: recēnsum populī … vīcātim per dominōs īnsulārum ēgit; Traupman 288: census, populī recēnsus

    Post-Augustan: Caesar’s street-by-street count of the people who drew free grain. Traupman’s word for a modern census.

  • populātiō, populātiōnis f. — laying waste, plundering

    noun, third declension · avoid · classical · Caes. BG 1.15.2: rapīnīs, pābulātiōnibus populātiōnibusque

    A false friend: from populor, “lay waste”. The sense “population” is late Latin, in one poet (Sedulius, Lewis & Short).

Examples

  • Mīlia octōgintā eō lūstrō cīvium cēnsa dīcuntur … Ad eam multitūdinem urbs quoque amplificanda vīsa est.

    Eighty thousand citizens are said to have been counted at that census … For a population of that size the city, too, seemed to need enlarging.Liv. 1.44.2–3

  • cum in spem magis futūrae multitūdinis quam ad id quod tum hominum erat mūnīrent

    for they built their walls for the population they hoped for rather than for the people they had thenLiv. 1.8.4

  • regiō überrimae multitūdinis

    a densely populated regionTraupman 203

  • numerus omnis multitūdinis

    the total number of the populationTraupman 363

See also people, town, city, state, community.
